chunks: And from him, from Abu Ja'far, from al-Husayn ibn Sa'id, from Muhammad ibn Abi Umayr, from Abd al-Rahman ibn al-Hajjaj, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) who said:

In five qilas (young camels), one sheep; and there is nothing in what is less than five. In ten, two sheep; in fifteen, three; in twenty, four; in twenty-five, five. In twenty-six, a ibnathu makhidh (one-year-old female camel) until thirty-five; if one more is added, then in it is an ibnathu labun (two-year-old female camel) until forty-four; if one more is added, then in it is a hiqqah (three-year-old female camel) until fifty; if one more is added, then in it is a jadha'ah (four-year-old female camel) until seventy-five; if one more is added, then in it are two ibnathu labun until ninety; if one more is added, then in it are two hiqqah until two hundred; when the camels become numerous, then in every fifty is a hiqqah.

key_terms.ابْنَةُ مَخَاض: A one-year-old female camel whose mother was pregnant when she was born
key_terms.قِلَاص: Young camels (specifically those between one and two years old, often used as the base unit for Zakat calculation)

ai.seo_question: What is the Zakat ruling for different numbers of camels in Shia jurisprudence?
ai.summary: This hadith from *Tahdhib al-Ahkam* elaborates on the *khums* of camels, detailing the precise age and gender classifications (such as *ibnat makhidh* and *hiqqah*) required for Zakat payment, a system foundational to Shia jurisprudence. It reflects the scholarly tradition of distinguishing between specific animal categories to ensure equitable distribution of alms, linking directly to the Quranic mandate for charitable giving.
